title: Policy rates are rising again: Bank Rate up to 4% in November 2026
what_happened: The Bank of England raised Bank Rate by 0.25pp to 4% (8-1; one member wanted 4.25%), its first increase since 2023, with CPI at 3.5% and projected near 5% by mid-2027. The Fed held at 3.75-4.00% on 28 Oct with two dissents for a hike; the ECB held its deposit rate at 2.50% after a September increase.
client_effect: Higher yields lower the present value of DB liabilities and of existing bonds; cash and money market yields rise; leveraged borrowers and floating-rate private credit face higher servicing costs; inflation-linked liabilities grow.
decision_that_changes: DB trustees: hedge ratios, collateral buffers, timing of buyout. Treasurers: how much to hold in MMFs versus term. Insurers: reinvestment yields versus credit risk. Wealth selectors: duration and cash allocations.
existing_investments: Mark-to-market losses on long-dated bonds; collateral calls on leveraged LDI (buffers are larger than in 2022); liquidity balances may grow.
possible_gsam_response: (Layer B, not a GS statement) Explain funding-level and collateral effects scheme by scheme; show liquidity and short-duration options; avoid presenting a rate view as certainty.
sales_angle: A reason to open a conversation about liquidity, inflation protection or collateral resilience, not proof that a product should be bought.
rm_angle: Proactive calls to existing clients on what the move did to their portfolio and hedges, before they ask.
risks_counterarguments: The inflation projection may prove wrong and policy could reverse; schemes that are well hedged may need to do nothing; higher cash yields compete with every fee-bearing product.
client_question: How did your funding level and collateral headroom move this month, and has that changed your timetable or your liquidity needs?
watch: 17 December 2026 MPC; gilt yields and index-linked breakevens; CPI prints; any LDI collateral stress reports.

title: Nuveen completes £9.9bn acquisition of Schroders
what_happened: Nuveen, TIAA's asset manager, completed its acquisition of Schroders plc (announced 12 Feb 2026). The combined firm reports about $2.6tn; Schroders operates separately within Nuveen for 12-18 months; London is the non-US headquarters.
client_effect: Clients of Schroders (including Schroders Solutions' fiduciary and LDI clients and wealth fund buyers) face a change of ownership and, later, possible team, product and system integration.
decision_that_changes: Trustees and fund selectors decide whether to review the mandate now, add a watch flag, or wait; consultants update manager ratings.
existing_investments: Mandates continue under existing contracts; change-of-control and key-person provisions may be reviewed.
possible_gsam_response: (Layer B, not a GS statement) Be ready with accurate, non-disparaging answers if a client or consultant launches a review; do not approach clients with speculation about a competitor.
sales_angle: A review, if it happens, is initiated by the client or consultant. The sales task is to be shortlisted on merit.
rm_angle: Existing Goldman clients may ask whether Goldman itself is stable; show continuity of people and process.
risks_counterarguments: Most clients do not move on ownership change alone; integration may improve Schroders' offer; Schroders reported positive client feedback; Goldman is also an acquirer (Innovator, NEOS, LCN) and can be asked the same question.
client_question: When a manager you use changes owner, what would you need to see over the next year to stay comfortable?
watch: Consultant rating changes; departures from Schroders Solutions; UK fiduciary retender announcements in 2027.

title: Asset-management consolidation accelerates in 2026
what_happened: Dealogic counted about $53.8bn of asset-management M&A in the year to late August 2026, including Nuveen-Schroders, a take-private of Janus Henderson, Victory Capital-First Eagle and Wellington-Hartford Funds; BNP Paribas integrated AXA IM; Goldman itself bought Innovator and agreed to buy NEOS and LCN.
client_effect: Fewer, larger managers; more frequent ownership changes for the funds and mandates clients hold; buyers of scale gain pricing power in passive but margins stay near 30%.
decision_that_changes: Whether to concentrate with large multi-capability firms or deliberately keep specialists; how often to review managers after ownership changes.
existing_investments: Fund mergers, share-class changes and team turnover at acquired firms.
possible_gsam_response: (Layer B, not a GS statement) Present breadth honestly, including where a specialist is the better answer.
sales_angle: Scale and stability arguments carry more weight with small investment teams.
rm_angle: Reassure on continuity; flag early any change that touches the client's mandate.
risks_counterarguments: Scale has not improved industry margins (BCG); integration often disrupts service; clients may respond by diversifying away from the largest firms.
client_question: Do you want fewer, deeper manager relationships, or do you see concentration with a few large firms as a risk?
watch: Further deals; consultant commentary on integration; regulatory review of concentration.

title: Fee compression continues while revenue depends on markets
what_happened: BCG: institutional fees have fallen about 3% a year; more than 80% of 2025 revenue growth came from market appreciation; costs grew faster than revenue from 2010 to 2025. Morningstar: US asset-weighted fund fees fell to 0.32% in 2025. IC Select: UK fiduciary fees fell 27% over five years.
client_effect: Clients pay less per pound managed and expect more service; they can credibly threaten to move to a cheaper provider.
decision_that_changes: Fee renegotiation at review; move from active to passive or active ETF; consolidation of mandates to reach breakpoints.
existing_investments: Existing mandates face repricing requests even when performance is fine.
possible_gsam_response: (Layer B, not a GS statement) Defend price with evidence of value, offer breakpoints or broader relationships, and accept that sometimes the cheaper product is the right answer.
sales_angle: Price is rarely the opening argument but must be competitive to reach the shortlist.
rm_angle: Fee conversations are an RM responsibility: prepare the value-for-money case before the client asks.
risks_counterarguments: Fees are observable and value is not, so pressure is structural; for small UK schemes fiduciary fees have actually risen, so the trend is not uniform.
client_question: When you last reviewed what you pay us, what did you compare it with, and what would you need to see to judge it good value?
watch: Morningstar and BCG annual fee studies; UK value-for-money framework for DC; consultant fee surveys.

title: AI moves into RFPs, meeting notes and reporting in distribution teams
what_happened: Cerulli: 81% of institutional sales and service teams use AI for RFP content and 77% for meeting notes; far fewer for prospecting or sales strategy. Mercer: 73% of managers use AI for operational efficiency; only 5% let it act autonomously. Isio: 85% of UK fiduciary managers use AI, mainly to draft reports and emails.
client_effect: Clients may receive faster, more consistent responses; they also ask how AI is governed and whether outputs are checked.
decision_that_changes: Due-diligence questionnaires now include AI governance; clients may shorten response deadlines.
possible_gsam_response: (Layer B, not a GS statement) Use the time saved for accuracy checks and client-specific analysis; be able to explain controls.
sales_angle: Faster proposal turnaround is now expected, so it no longer differentiates on its own.
rm_angle: Automated reporting raises the bar for the human explanation that accompanies it.
risks_counterarguments: Survey figures are self-reported and partly vendor-sponsored; errors in AI-drafted answers create liability; no evidence yet on junior hiring effects; BCG's 25-35% cost-saving figure is an estimate.
client_question: What do you want to know about how we use AI in the material we send you, and where would you want a named person accountable?
watch: Regulatory guidance on AI in client communications; Cerulli/Mercer follow-up surveys; reported headcount changes in distribution.

title: Private credit under strain: elevated redemptions in retail semi-liquid funds
what_happened: The Bank of England's July 2026 Financial Stability Report said risky credit markets including private credit remain vulnerable to tighter financing conditions and that redemption requests have been elevated in several retail funds, with some limiting redemptions. Blackstone reported BCRED redemption requests stayed elevated in Q3 2026 even as private-wealth AUM reached $330bn.
client_effect: Wealth clients in semi-liquid funds may be unable to redeem on demand; insurers and pension funds reassess valuation and liquidity assumptions; rising rates add pressure on borrowers.
decision_that_changes: Fund selectors tighten due diligence on liquidity terms, valuation policy and leverage; some pause new allocations; insurers review capital treatment.
existing_investments: Holders of evergreen private credit funds face queues or gates; marks may lag.
possible_gsam_response: (Layer B, not a GS statement) Lead with liquidity terms and downside cases; do not sell semi-liquid as liquid; be explicit about who the product does not suit.
sales_angle: Selling private markets to wealth now requires proving the client understands redemption limits.
rm_angle: Tell holders early how redemption queues work and what the fund has done; this is where trust is tested.
risks_counterarguments: Stress is concentrated in particular funds and borrowers; private wealth inflows continue (Blackstone BXPE record quarter); the BoE judges households and corporates resilient in aggregate.
client_question: If you could not redeem for four quarters, would this allocation still be the right size for your clients?
watch: BoE December 2026 FSR; redemption data from large evergreen funds; default rates; FCA/ESMA action on semi-liquid funds.

title: UK fiduciary management: fewer mandates, larger ones, falling fees at the top
what_happened: UK fiduciary assets are above £250bn (+58% in three years) but the number of mandates fell 4% in the year to June 2025, the first fall since 2008, as schemes buy out. OCIO-style mandates are 6% by number and 53% of DB fiduciary AUM. Fees above £500m are falling; below £50m they rose. Providers are consolidating (Mercer-Cardano, Nuveen-Schroders) and Columbia Threadneedle exited.
client_effect: Large schemes have many bidders and pricing power; small schemes have fewer bidders. About 26% of fully delegated schemes expect buyout within three years, which ends the mandate.
decision_that_changes: Whether to delegate fully, partially or not at all; whether to run on or buy out; whether to pay for independent oversight (only one in three do).
existing_investments: Existing fiduciary mandates shrink or terminate at buyout: a good client outcome that removes fee revenue.
possible_gsam_response: (Layer B, not a GS statement) Compete where bespoke capability matters (£1bn+); be clear about the endgame path and what happens to fees when the scheme buys out.
sales_angle: Few, very large, slow competitive tenders run by third-party evaluators; losing after months of work is normal.
rm_angle: Help the scheme reach its endgame even though success ends the relationship; propose oversight rather than resist it.
risks_counterarguments: Goldman's UK share is not public; consultant-heritage providers hold about half of mandates by number; run-on with surplus release could slow buyouts (scenario).
client_question: Is your endgame buyout or run-on, and how should your fiduciary manager be paid in a way that does not reward delaying it?
watch: Isio, IC Select, XPS and Quantum annual surveys; large mandate announcements; Pension Schemes Act surplus rules (see R3).

title: Public-private alliances and active ETFs reshape products for wealth intermediaries
what_happened: Wellington, Vanguard and Blackstone launched two public-private funds (US, July 2026); Capital Group and KKR took a public-private credit fund to Europe and Asia-Pacific via HSBC Private Bank (May 2026); Goldman agreed a T. Rowe Price partnership (Sept 2025). European active ETF assets reached about EUR 117bn at end Q3 2026, with J.P. Morgan holding about 41%; passive ETFs took about 57% of Q3 2026 European fund flows.
client_effect: Fund selectors face more wrappers for similar exposures and must judge liquidity and layered fees; shelf space goes to firms with distribution access.
decision_that_changes: Which vehicle (mutual fund, active ETF, evergreen fund, model portfolio) goes on the approved list; how many private-market providers to carry.
existing_investments: Mutual fund holdings may be switched to cheaper ETF share classes or models.
possible_gsam_response: (Layer B, not a GS statement) Offer the client's preferred wrapper where it exists; be honest where a competitor leads (for example active ETFs).
sales_angle: Approved-list placement is the start: funded assets depend on adviser adoption afterwards.
rm_angle: Support advisers with training and reporting so listed funds are actually used and held appropriately.
risks_counterarguments: Active ETFs are still about 3.4% of European ETF assets; alliance funds are small at launch; fee levels are lower than the vehicles they replace (BCG).
client_question: Which wrapper do your advisers actually use for new money now, and what would make a fund you already list easier to hold?
watch: Morningstar active ETF data; European launches by the alliances; platform shelf changes.

title: Global managers build presence around Gulf sovereign investors
what_happened: Fourteen firms announced plans for an Abu Dhabi Global Market presence in October 2026; managers there oversee more than $2.1tn globally; Capital Group obtained an ADGM licence. BlackRock is reported to plan up to $100bn of deployment via the region; Mubadala and ADIA are reported to partner with Apollo, Blue Owl and KKR in private credit; PIF anchors new vehicles for managers that open in Riyadh.
client_effect: Sovereign investors can ask for local presence, co-investment, knowledge transfer and anchor terms; they are partners and competitors for deals as well as clients.
decision_that_changes: Which managers receive mandates or anchor commitments, and on what conditions (local office, joint ventures).
existing_investments: Existing mandates may be consolidated into strategic partnerships.
possible_gsam_response: (Layer B, not a GS statement) Coverage needs partnership structures and senior access, not product pushing; local regulation and presence matter.
sales_angle: Long, relationship-led cycles with bespoke terms; origination credit is shared across the firm.
rm_angle: Servicing includes training, secondments and co-investment flow, beyond reporting.
risks_counterarguments: Regional conflict in 2026 has affected sentiment (BoE refers to the Middle East conflict); headline commitment figures are not funded assets; Goldman-specific Gulf evidence is outside this stream (see R5).
client_question: Beyond returns, what do you want a manager to build with you locally?
watch: ADGM/DIFC/Riyadh licence announcements; sovereign fund annual reports; anchor mandates.

title: Tokenised money market fund shares as collateral
what_happened: BNY and Goldman Sachs launched 'mirror' tokens of MMF shares on Goldman's digital asset platform in July 2025, with funds from BlackRock, Fidelity, Federated Hermes, BNY Dreyfus and GSAM. In July 2026 an industry group (GDF with ISDA) published sandbox work on using tokenised MMFs as collateral.
client_effect: Treasurers and pension funds could post MMF shares as margin instead of redeeming to cash, reducing forced selling in stress.
decision_that_changes: Whether to hold liquidity in vehicles that can be mobilised as collateral; operational readiness and legal certainty.
existing_investments: No change yet for most holders; adoption volumes not established.
possible_gsam_response: (Layer B, not a GS statement) Explain what is live versus pilot; keep the focus on the client's liquidity and collateral problem.
sales_angle: A talking point with sophisticated treasury and LDI clients, not yet a mainstream product decision.
rm_angle: Help operations teams understand eligibility and custody implications.
risks_counterarguments: Legal and regulatory acceptance of tokenised collateral is incomplete; competitors participate in the same programme, so it is not exclusive; volumes may stay small.
client_question: In a margin call, how quickly can you turn your liquidity holdings into eligible collateral today?
watch: Regulatory statements on tokenised collateral eligibility; reported volumes; UK and EU MMF reform implementation.
